section.heading: 4.2. Applications of the Second Derivative
Determining the Intervals of Concavity
section.paragraph: Consider the graphs shown in Figure 26, which give the estimated population of the world and of the United States through the year 2000. Both graphs are rising, indicating that both the U.S. population and the world population continued to increase through the year 2000. But observe that the graph in Figure 26a opens upward, whereas the graph in Figure 26b opens downward. What is the significance of this? To answer this question, let’s look at the slopes of the tangent lines to various points on each graph (Figure 27).

section.paragraph: In Figure 27a, we see that the slopes of the tangent lines to the graph are increasing as we move from left to right. Since the slope of the tangent line to the graph at a point on the graph measures the rate of change of the function at that point, we conclude that the world population not only was increasing through the year 2000 but also was increasing at an increasing pace. A similar analysis of Figure 27b reveals that the U.S. population was increasing, but at a decreasing pace.
The shape of a curve can be described by using the notion of concavity.

note.title: Concavity of a Function f
note.heading: Concavity of a Function f
note.paragraph: Let the function $$f$$ be differentiable on an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ . Then,

list.item: The graph of $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ if $$f^{\prime}$$ is increasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
The graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ if $$f^{\prime}$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

section.paragraph: Geometrically, a curve is concave upward if it lies above its tangent lines (Figure 28a). Similarly, a curve is concave downward if it lies below its tangent lines (Figure 28b).

image.alt: Details Two graphs a and b, each plot a curve on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis has tick marks labeled a and b. In graph a, two vertical lines are drawn perpendicular to the x axis meet at the labeled marks a and b. The U shaped curve starts very close and to the right of the line, slopes downward to the right, concave up, reaches the low point, from where it turns upward to the right, still concave up and reaches to the left of the vertical line. Four slanting lines are drawn at the turning point to the left side of the curve; two on the left side of the curve and two on the right such that the curve lies above the tangent lines. The tangent at the lower part of the curve rises gradually upward to the right and the tangent at the upper part of the curve rises even more steeply upward to the right. In graph b, the inverted U shaped curve starts above the horizontal axis, slopes upward to the right, follows almost a linear path, then it slightly concave down, after it inflects, slopes downward, follows almost a linear path. Two vertical lines drawn from the entry point and end point of the curve to meet the x axis labeled at marks a and b. Four slanting lines are drawn at the turning point to the left side of the curve; two on the left side of the curve and two on the right such that the curve lies below the tangent lines. The tangent at the lower part of the curve rises gradually upward to the right and the tangent at the upper part of the curve rises even more steeply upward to the right.

section.paragraph: We also say that the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward at a number $$c$$ if there exists an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ containing $$c$$ on which the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward. Similarly, we say that the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward at a number $$c$$ if there exists an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ containing $$c$$ on which the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward.

If a function $$f$$ has a second derivative $$f^{''}$$ , we can use $$f^{''}$$ to determine the intervals of concavity of the graph of the function. Recall that $$f^{''}(x)$$ measures the rate of change of the slope $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$\left( {x,f(x)} \right)$$ . Thus, if $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ on an interval $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then the slopes of the tangent lines to the graph of $$f$$ are increasing on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , so the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ . Similarly, if $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ . These observations suggest the following theorem.

list.item: If $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ for every value of $$x$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .
If $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ for every value of $$x$$ in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ .

section.paragraph: The following procedure, based on the conclusions of Theorem 2, may be used to determine the intervals of concavity of the graph of a function.

If $$f^{''}(c) > 0$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward on that interval. If $$f^{''}(c) < 0$$ , then the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on that interval.

section.heading: Inflection Points
section.paragraph: Figure 33 shows the total sales $$S$$ of a manufacturer of automobile air conditioners versus the amount of money $$x$$ that the company spends on advertising its product.

image.alt: Details A curve y = S(x) is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The x axis ranges from 0 to over 100 (thousands of dollars) with the tick marks on the x axis increasing in increments of 20. The y axis ranges from 0 to over 5000 (thousands of dollars) with the tick marks on the y axis increasing in increments of 1000. The curve begins with a low at the y axis, very close to the origin, slightly above it, goes up to the right, concave up and reaches its point of inflection at a point marked (50, 2700) and then continues to rise upward to the right, now concave down, till it reaches its high point at around (100, 5000).

figure.caption: The graph of $$S$$ has a point of inflection at $$\left( {50,2700} \right)$$ .

section.paragraph: Notice that the graph of the continuous function $$y = S(x)$$ changes concavity—from upward to downward—at the point $$\left( {50,2700} \right)$$ . This point is called an inflection point of $$S$$ . To understand the significance of this inflection point, observe that the total sales increase rather slowly at first, but as more money is spent on advertising, the total sales increase rapidly. This rapid increase reflects the effectiveness of the company’s ads. However, a point is soon reached after which any additional advertising expenditure results in increased sales but at a slower rate of increase. This point, commonly known as the point of diminishing returns, is the point of inflection of the function $$S$$ . We will return to this example later.
Let’s now state formally the definition of an inflection point.

note.title: Inflection Point
note.heading: Inflection Point
note.paragraph: A point on the graph of a continuous function $$f$$ where the tangent line exists and where the concavity changes is called a point of inflection or an inflection point .

section.paragraph: Observe that the graph of a function crosses its tangent line at a point of inflection (Figure 34).

section.paragraph: The following procedure may be used to find inflection points:

list.item: Compute $$f^{''}(x)$$ .
Determine the numbers in the domain of $$f$$ for which $$f^{''}(x) = 0$$ or $$f^{''}(x)$$ does not exist.

Determine the sign of $$f^{''}(x)$$ to the left and right of each number $$c$$ found in Step 2. If there is a change in the sign of $$f^{''}(x)$$ as we move across $$x = c$$ , then $$\left( {c,f(c)} \right)$$ is an inflection point of $$f$$ .

section.paragraph: The numbers that were found in Step 2 are only candidates for the inflection points of $$f$$ . For example, you can easily verify that $$f^{''}(0) = 0$$ if $$f(x) = x^{4}$$ , but a sketch of the graph of $$f$$ will show that $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ is not an inflection point.

section.paragraph: The next example uses an interpretation of the first and second derivatives to help us sketch the graph of a function.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Sketch the graph of a function having the following properties:

$$\begin{array}{ll} & \begin{array}{rcl} {f\left( {- 1} \right)} & = & 4 \\ {f(0)} & = & 2 \\ {f(1)} & = & 0 \\ {f^{\prime}\left( {- 1} \right)} & = & 0 \\ {f^{\prime}(1)} & = & 0 \end{array} \\ \begin{array}{l} {f^{\prime}(x) > 0} \\ {f^{\prime}(x) < 0} \\ {f^{''}(x) < 0} \\ {f^{''}(x) > 0} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} {{on}\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right){and}\left( {1,\infty} \right)} \\ {{on}\left( {- 1,1} \right)} \\ {{on}\left( {- \infty,0} \right)} \\ {{on}\left( {0,\infty} \right)} \end{array} \end{array}$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: First, we plot the points $$\left( {- 1,4} \right)$$ , $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ that lie on the graph of $$f$$ . Since $$f^{\prime}\left( {- 1} \right) = 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}(1) = 0$$ , the tangent lines at the points $$\left( {- 1,4} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ are horizontal. Since $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ , we see that $$f$$ has a relative maximum at the point $$\left( {- 1,4} \right)$$ . Also, $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ and $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ on $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ implies that $$f$$ has a relative minimum at the point $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ (Figure 41a).

Since $$f^{''}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and $$f^{''}(x) > 0$$ on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ , we see that the point $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ is an inflection point. Finally, we complete the graph, making use of the fact that $$f$$ is increasing on $$\left( {- \infty, - 1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,\infty} \right)$$ , where it is given that $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ , and $$f$$ is decreasing on $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ , where $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ . Also, make sure that the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and concave upward on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ (Figure 41b).

section.heading: The Second Derivative Test
section.paragraph: We now show how the second derivative $$f^{''}$$ of a function $$f$$ can be used to help us determine whether a critical number of $$f$$ gives rise to a relative extremum of $$f$$ . Figure 43a shows the graph of a function that has a relative maximum at $$x = c$$ . Observe that the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward at that number. Similarly, Figure 43b shows that at a relative minimum of $$f$$ , the graph is concave upward. But from our previous work, we know that the graph of $$f$$ is concave downward at $$x = c$$ if $$f^{''}(c) < 0$$ and the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward at $$x = c$$ if $$f^{''}(c) > 0$$ . These observations suggest the following alternative procedure for determining whether a critical number of $$f$$ gives rise to a relative extremum of $$f$$ . This result is called the Second Derivative Test and is applicable when $$f^{''}$$ exists.

Find all the critical numbers of $$f$$ at which $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ .

Compute $$f^{''}(c)$$ for each such critical number $$c$$ . If $$f^{''}(c) < 0$$ , then $$f$$ has a relative maximum at $$c$$ . If $$f^{''}(c) > 0$$ , then $$f$$ has a relative minimum at $$c$$ . If $$f^{''}(c) = 0$$ or $$f^{''}(c)$$ does not exist, the test fails; that is, it is inconclusive.

note.paragraph: The Second Derivative Test does not yield a conclusion if $$f^{''}(c) = 0$$ or if $$f^{''}(c)$$ does not exist. In other words, $$x = c$$ may or may not give rise to a relative extremum (see Exercise 110). In such cases, you should revert to the First Derivative Test.

section.heading: Comparing the First and Second Derivative Tests
section.paragraph: Notice that both the First Derivative Test and the Second Derivative Test are used to classify the critical numbers of $$f$$ . What are the pros and cons of the two tests? Since the Second Derivative Test is applicable only when $$f^{''}$$ exists, it is less versatile than the First Derivative Test. For example, it cannot be used to locate the relative minimum $$f(0) = 0$$ of the function $$f(x) = x^{2 \slash 3}$$ .

Furthermore, the Second Derivative Test is inconclusive when $$f^{''}$$ is equal to zero at a critical number of $$f$$ , whereas the First Derivative Test always yields a conclusion; that is, it tells us if $$f$$ has a relative maximum, relative minimum, or neither. The Second Derivative Test is also inconvenient to use when $$f^{''}$$ is difficult to compute. On the plus side, if $$f^{''}$$ is computed easily, then we use the Second Derivative Test, since it involves just the evaluation of $$f^{''}$$ at the critical number(s) of $$f$$ . Also, the conclusions of the Second Derivative Test are important in theoretical work.

We close this section by summarizing the different roles played by the first derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ and the second derivative $$f^{''}$$ of a function $$f$$ in determining the properties of the graph of $$f$$ . The first derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ tells us where $$f$$ is increasing and where $$f$$ is decreasing, whereas the second derivative $$f^{''}$$ tells us where the graph of $$f$$ is concave upward and where it is concave downward. These different properties of $$f$$ are reflected by the signs of $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$f^{''}$$ in the interval of interest.
